cemc-hypatia-2012-01b.title: Find TR, then use base PR
cemc-hypatia-2012-01b.body:
In right triangle $QTR$, $TR^2 = 51^2 - 24^2 = 2601 - 576 = 2025$, so $TR = 45$. Then $PR = 32 + 45 = 77$, and $QT$ is the height to base $PR$:
$$\text{Area} = \tfrac12 \times 77 \times 24 = 924.$$

**Answer: 924**

cemc-hypatia-2012-01b.title: Add two right triangles
cemc-hypatia-2012-01b.body:
$\triangle PQR$ is the union of right triangles $PTQ$ and $QTR$: areas $\frac12 \cdot 32 \cdot 24 = 384$ and $\frac12 \cdot 45 \cdot 24 = 540$ (with $TR = 45$ from the $8$-$15$-$17$ triple scaled by $3$: $24, 45, 51$). Total $384 + 540 = 924$.

**Answer: 924**

cemc-hypatia-2012-01c.title: Recognize triples
cemc-hypatia-2012-01c.body:
With $TS = 60$ (as in the first approach):
- $\triangle PTS$: legs $32 = 4 \cdot 8$, $60 = 4 \cdot 15$, so $PS = 4 \cdot 17 = 68$.
- $\triangle RTS$: legs $45 = 15 \cdot 3$, $60 = 15 \cdot 4$, so $RS = 15 \cdot 5 = 75$.

Perimeter $= 40 + 51 + 75 + 68 = 234$.

**Answer: 234**

cemc-hypatia-2012-02a.title: Area picture
cemc-hypatia-2012-02a.body:
A square of side $a + b$ splits into squares $a^2$, $b^2$ and two rectangles $ab$. So its area is $24 + 6 + 6 = 36$.

**Answer: 36**

cemc-hypatia-2012-02c.title: Find j and k
cemc-hypatia-2012-02c.body:
$j$ and $k$ are roots of $t^2 - 6t + jk = 0$. With $jk = -8$: $t = 3 \pm \sqrt{17}$, and indeed $(3 + \sqrt{17})^2 + (3 - \sqrt{17})^2 = 2(9 + 17) = 52$. ✓

**Answer: $-8$**

cemc-hypatia-2012-02d.title: Check both values occur
cemc-hypatia-2012-02d.body:
From $m^2 + n^2 = 12$ and $m^2 n^2 = 4$, the numbers $m^2, n^2$ are the roots of $t^2 - 12t + 4 = 0$, i.e. $6 \pm 4\sqrt2$, both positive. So real $m, n$ exist, e.g. $m = \sqrt{6 + 4\sqrt2} = 2 + \sqrt2$, $n = \pm\sqrt{6 - 4\sqrt2} = \pm(2 - \sqrt2)$. Then $mn = \pm(4 - 2) = \pm 2$: both signs really occur.

**Answer: $mn = \pm 2$**

cemc-hypatia-2012-03a.title: Perpendicular slopes
cemc-hypatia-2012-03a.body:
The slope of $OM$ is $\frac{1/4}{1/2} = \frac12$ and the slope of $ON$ is $\frac{n^2}{n} = n$ ($n \ne 0$). Perpendicular lines have slopes multiplying to $-1$: $\frac12 n = -1$, so $n = -2$.

**Answer: $-2$**

cemc-hypatia-2012-03a.title: Pythagorean check
cemc-hypatia-2012-03a.body:
$\angle MON = 90^\circ$ means $OM^2 + ON^2 = MN^2$:
$$\tfrac14 + \tfrac1{16} + n^2 + n^4 = (n - \tfrac12)^2 + (n^2 - \tfrac14)^2 = n^4 + \tfrac{n^2}{2} - n + \tfrac14 + \tfrac1{16}.$$
Cancelling gives $\frac{n^2}{2} + n = 0$, i.e. $n(n + 2) = 0$, so $n = -2$ (as $n \ne 0$).

**Answer: $-2$**

cemc-hypatia-2012-03b.title: Perpendicular slopes
cemc-hypatia-2012-03b.body:
The slope of $BA$ is $\frac{b^2 - 4}{b - 2} = b + 2$ (as $b \ne 2$), and the slope of $BO$ is $\frac{b^2}{b} = b$ (as $b \ne 0$). For a right angle at $B$: $b(b + 2) = -1$, i.e. $b^2 + 2b + 1 = 0$, $(b + 1)^2 = 0$, so $b = -1$.

**Answer: $-1$**

cemc-hypatia-2012-03b.title: Dot product
cemc-hypatia-2012-03b.body:
The vectors $\vec{BA} = (2 - b, 4 - b^2)$ and $\vec{BO} = (-b, -b^2)$ must be perpendicular:
$$-b(2 - b) - b^2(4 - b^2) = -b(2 - b)\left[1 + b(2 + b)\right] = 0.$$
Since $b \ne 0, 2$, we need $b^2 + 2b + 1 = 0$, so $b = -1$. Check: $B = (-1, 1)$, $\vec{BA} = (3, 3)$, $\vec{BO} = (1, -1)$, dot product $0$. ✓

**Answer: $-1$**

cemc-hypatia-2012-03c.title: Slopes on a parabola
cemc-hypatia-2012-03c.body:
The slope of the chord joining $(u, u^2)$ and $(v, v^2)$ is $\frac{u^2 - v^2}{u - v} = u + v$.

So $QP$ has slope $p + q$ and $QR$ has slope $r + q$. Since $\angle PQR = 90^\circ$,
$$(p + q)(r + q) = -1.$$
Both factors are integers, so one is $1$ and the other is $-1$. Either way their sum is $0$: $(p + q) + (r + q) = 0$, i.e. $2q + p + r = 0$. ∎

(Neither chord can be vertical, since points on the parabola have distinct $x$-coordinates.)

cemc-hypatia-2012-04a.title: List the divisors
cemc-hypatia-2012-04a.body:
The divisors of $2p^2$ ($p$ an odd prime) are $1, 2, p, 2p, p^2, 2p^2$, so
$$S(2p^2) = 3 + 3p + 3p^2 = 2613 \implies p^2 + p - 870 = 0 \implies (p - 29)(p + 30) = 0.$$
So $p = 29$.

**Answer: 29**

cemc-hypatia-2012-04a.title: Factor the divisor sum
cemc-hypatia-2012-04a.body:
The divisors pair up as $\{1, 2\} \times \{1, p, p^2\}$, so $S(2p^2) = (1 + 2)(1 + p + p^2)$. Then $1 + p + p^2 = 871$. Since $29^2 = 841$ and $841 + 29 + 1 = 871$, $p = 29$ (and $p^2 + p$ is increasing, so this is the only one).

**Answer: 29**

cemc-hypatia-2012-04b.title: Set up two equations
cemc-hypatia-2012-04b.body:
For primes $p, q > 3$: $S(2p) = 1 + 2 + p + 2p = 3p + 3$ and $S(9q) = 1 + 3 + 9 + q + 3q + 9q = 13q + 13$. So $3p + 3 = 13q + 13$, i.e.
$$3p - 13q = 10.$$
Consecutive means $m - n = \pm 1$.

**Case $2p - 9q = 1$.** Multiply by $3$: $6p - 27q = 3$; double the first equation: $6p - 26q = 20$. Subtracting, $q = 17$, then $2p = 154$ and $p = 77 = 7 \times 11$, not prime. No solution.

**Case $9q - 2p = 1$.** $27q - 6p = 3$ and $6p - 26q = 20$; adding, $q = 23$, then $3p = 10 + 299 = 309$ and $p = 103$, which is prime.

So $m = 206$, $n = 207$. Check: $S(206) = 312$ and $S(207) = 13 \cdot 24 = 312$. ✓

**Answer: $(m, n) = (206, 207)$**

cemc-hypatia-2012-04c.title: Count directly using remainders
cemc-hypatia-2012-04c.body:
$S = (p + 1)(p^2 + 1)(q + 1)$. Note $3 \nmid p^2 + 1$ always, so the factor $3$ must come from $p + 1$ or $q + 1$, i.e. $p \equiv 2$ or $q \equiv 2 \pmod 3$.

**Both odd.** Then $p + 1$, $p^2 + 1$, $q + 1$ are all even, so $8 \mid S$. Hence $24 \nmid S$ exactly when neither $p$ nor $q$ is $\equiv 2 \pmod 3$, i.e. both lie in $\{3, 7, 13, 19\}$: $4 \times 3 = 12$ pairs.

**$p = 2$.** $S = 15(q + 1)$, divisible by $24$ iff $8 \mid q + 1$, i.e. $q \in \{7, 23\}$. So $9 - 2 = 7$ pairs fail.

**$q = 2$.** $S = 3(p + 1)(p^2 + 1)$ with $p$ odd. Since $p^2 + 1 \equiv 2 \pmod 4$, we need $4 \mid p + 1$, i.e. $p \equiv 3 \pmod 4$: $p \in \{3, 7, 11, 19, 23\}$. The other $4$ primes ($5, 13, 17, 29$) fail.

Total: $12 + 7 + 4 = 23$.

**Answer: 23**
